rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Joseph a noble angel describes beauty at the highest level, reflecting the intuition that nothing living is more beautiful than an angel or uglier than Satan; the cited Arabic poems extend the comparison.
rows.anchor: وغرضهن من هذا وصفه بأنه في أقصى مراتب الحسن والكمال الملائم لطباعهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not prove angels superior to human beings, contrary to Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī and his followers, whom Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī supported; al-Ālūsī dismisses that support.
rows.anchor: أن الآية لا تقوم دليلا على أن الملك أفضل من بني آدم كما ظن أبو علي الجبائي وأتباعه وأيده الفخر

rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: Some say the women began by declaring God free of evil, then exonerated Joseph, making their denial emphatic; al-Ālūsī prefers the beauty reading on context, while this usage is clear at 12:51.
rows.anchor: وذهب غير واحد إلى أن الغرض تنزيهه عليه السلام عما رمي به على أكمل وجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers the description of Joseph's extraordinary beauty because the context before and after supports it; the phrase is plainly exculpatory in the women's later statement.
rows.anchor: والمنصور ما أشير إليه أولا وهو الذي يقتضيه السياق والسباق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Hijazi dialect mā works like laysa; al-Raḍī allows negation of past and future as well as present. Hijazis usually put the predicate after bāʾ, while Tamim raises it.
rows.anchor: عاملة عمل ليس وهي لغة للحجازيين لمشابهتها لها في نفي الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammarians found only a poetic witness for an accusative predicate in Hijazi speech; Tamimi usage raises it, as illustrated by another verse.
rows.anchor: حتى أن النحويين لم يجدوا شاهدا على النصب في أشعارهم غير قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya claims no one read the verse in the Hijazi dialect here, although al-Ālūsī also reports Ibn Masʿūd's reading in that dialect.
rows.anchor: وزعم ابن عطية أنه لم يقرأ بها أحد هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd read the Hijazi form; al-Ālūsī identifies the dialectal reading before introducing readings with bāʾ by al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Ḥuwayrith.
rows.anchor: وبلغتهم قرأ ابن مسعود رضي الله تعالى عنه

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو الحويرث الحنفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Ḥuwayrith read bi-sharāʾ, taking shirāʾ as a verbal noun for something purchasable: Joseph is too precious to be bought.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو الحويرث الحنفي ما هذا بشرى بالباء الجارة وكسر الشين

rows.speaker: عبد الوارث عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Wārith also transmitted the reading from Abū ʿAmr, with a report that the lām of malak was kasra; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports that vocalization from al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Ḥuwayrith too, linking the clauses as a kingly-status comparison.
rows.anchor: وروى هذه القراءة عبد الوارث عن أبي عمرو وأيضا إلا أنه روي عنه أنه مع ذلك كسر اللام من ملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in fa-dhālikunna is explanatory; the demonstrative points to Joseph as a man of beauty beyond human ranks, or to the one whose sight made the women cut their hands.
rows.anchor: الفاء فصيحة والخطاب للنسوة والإشارة حسبما يقتضيه الظاهر إلى يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative and relative clause mean that this is the noble angel or the man they saw, cut their hands for, and blamed her for loving.
rows.anchor: فذلكن الملك الكريم الخارج في الحسن عن المراتب البشرية أو الذي قطعتن أيديكن بسببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the demonstrative as the Canaanite slave the women had imagined; after seeing him, they know whom they blamed her for loving.
rows.anchor: العبد الكنعاني الذي صورتن في أنفسكن ثم لمتنني فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says they had not pictured Joseph truly; if they had seen his real beauty, they would have excused her infatuation.
rows.anchor: لو صورتنه بما عاينتن لعذرتنني في الافتتان به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A distant demonstrative for a present person can exalt his beauty and mark his rarity; it may reflect his absence at the earlier blame, while the idea he was kept away now to prevent temptation is remote.
rows.anchor: رفعا لمنزلته في الحسن واستبعادا لمحله فيه وإشارة إلى أنه لغرابته بعيد أن يوجد مثله

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows the demonstrative to refer to love of Joseph, with the pronoun in fīhi returning to that love; al-Ālūsī finds this remote.
rows.anchor: وجوز ابن عطية كون الإشارة إلى حب يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife confesses the remainder of her secret after establishing her case before the women; they had now experienced the attraction that affected her.
rows.anchor: وهو إباحة منها ببقية سرها بعد أن أقامت عليهن الحجة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses istaʿṣama as seeking and holding fast to protection, and disobeying her.
rows.anchor: أي طلب العصمة وتمسك بها وعصاني

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf says the intensive form istaʿṣama conveys emphatic refusal and strenuous self-restraint, like istamsaka and istawsaʿa.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف أن الاستعصام بناءا مبالغة يدل على الامتناع البليغ

rows.speaker: الصوفيون
rows.claim: The mystics say istaʿṣama is equivalent to iʿtaṣama, meaning he refrained from what she wanted; other forms similarly match iftiʿāl in meaning.
rows.anchor: أنه موافق لإعتصم وأما استمسك واستوسع واستجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿiṣma here means lexical restraint, not the later technical meaning of divine protection from inclination to sin.
rows.anchor: وليس المراد بالعصمة ما أودعه الله تعالى في بعض أنبيائه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes istaʿṣama as his flight: Joseph first refused verbally, then fled when speech did not stop her, seeking protection through escape.
rows.anchor: قيل : وعنث بذلك فراره عليه السلام منها فإنه امتنع منها أولا بالمقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the women already knew she tried to seduce him, she swears to her confession to show her delight in admitting it.
rows.anchor: مما تحدث به النسوة لإظهار ابتهاجها بذلك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says the oath especially emphasizes Joseph's refusal because youth, closeness, and her pressure made resistance seem unlikely; al-Ālūsī calls this unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه باعتبار المعطوف وهو الاستعصام كأنها نظمته لقوة الداعي إلى خلافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects that rationale as unconvincing and says the verse proves Joseph did not commit the scandalous act attributed by storytellers, rebuking al-Suddī for the tale of his undressing.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دليل على أنه عليه السلام لم يصدر منه ما سود به القصاص وجوه الطروس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In mā āmuruhu, mā is relative and its preposition is omitted; the object of āmara may be left implicit or inferred from yufʿal, with other staged analyses of the pronouns.
rows.anchor: فما موصولة والجملة بعدها صلة والعائد الهاء وقد حذف حرف الجر منه فاتصل بالفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poetic line illustrates the common omission of the preposition after āmara; her expression 'what I command' displays her assumed authority.
rows.anchor: وهذا أمر شائع مع أمر كقوله : أمرتك الخير فافعل ما أمرت به

rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munīr says the omitted preposition has become conventional, so the pronoun should be treated as an unattached accusative; two pronouns of the same type cannot attach together.
rows.anchor: إن هذا الجار مما أنس حذفه فلا يقدر العائد إلا منصوبا مفصولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā may instead be a verbal noun, with the pronoun referring to Joseph; carrying out an order means doing what it entails, by figurative attribution or an implied noun.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون ( ما ) مصدرية فالضمير المذكور ليوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She describes her solicitation as an order to display her assumed authority; li-yusjananna has a heavy nūn and passive form, fitting royal usage.
rows.anchor: وعبرت عن مراودتها بالأمر إظهار لجريان حكومتها عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive may also suggest imprisonment will follow immediately, as though no agent intervenes between her command and its execution.
rows.anchor: إيهاما لسرعة ترتب ذلك على عدم امتثاله لأمرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṣāghirīn means the humiliated and lowly; ṣaghar describes rank, while ṣaghura concerns bodily size, with several verbal nouns reported.
rows.anchor: أي الأذلال المهانين وهو من صغر كفرح ومصدر صغر بفتحتين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says the heavy nūn emphasizes certain imprisonment while a light nūn marks uncertain humiliation; another says humiliation follows imprisonment, so light emphasis suffices.
rows.anchor: قيل : لتحققه وما بعده بالنون الخفيفة لأنه غير متحقق

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group read both verbs with heavy nūn, contrary to the written form; the alif represents the pause form, as in al-Aʿshā's cited line.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة بالتثقيل فيهما وهو مخالف لرسم المصحف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says she earlier threatened painful punishment while angry and denying her advances, but now hopes to excuse herself, so she threatens prison; other views compare humiliation with the earlier torment, and the joined penalties here may be harsher.
rows.anchor: قيل : ولم تذكر العذاب الأليم الذي ذكرته في ( ما جزاء من أراد بأهلك سوءا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She intensifies the threat before the women to vent anger at Joseph's steadfastness and show him she fears no one, limiting their ability to advise him to comply.
rows.anchor: ولعلها إنما بالغت في ذلك بمحضر من تلك النسوة لمزيد غيظها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is unrestricted: while in prison, the two never receive food without Joseph describing its nature and qualities before it arrives.
rows.anchor: في الحبس حسب عادتكما المطردة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʾwīl is a metaphor for disclosing food's nature, like interpreting an obscure matter or dream, not the eventual outcome of a statement.
rows.anchor: استثناء مفرغ من أعم الأحوال أي لا يأتيكما طعام في حال من الأحوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling this disclosure taʾwīl is apt because food unknown to the prisoners resembles an obscure dream that needs interpretation.
rows.anchor: بالنسبة إلى الطعام المبهم بمنزلة التأويل بالنسبة إلى ما رؤي في المنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The metaphor echoes the prisoners' phrase, nabbiʾnā bi-taʾwīlihi; taking taʾwīl as the final outcome of words is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: ويحسن هذه الاستعارة ما في ذلك من المشاكلة لما وقع في عبارتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph intends to introduce and commend monotheism before answering their request to interpret the dreams.
rows.anchor: وكأنه عليه السلام أراد أن يعرض عليهما التوحيد ويزينه لهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wise adviser should first guide and counsel someone toward what is more important, then answer the question; Joseph may have been obligated to do this.
rows.anchor: مع الجهلة والفسقة إذا استفتاه واحد منهم أن يقدم الإرشاد والنصيحة أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He presents foreknowledge as a rhetorical bridge: food relates to their dream question, and extraordinary knowledge helps establish his truth and prophethood; mentioning useful knowledge of oneself is not forbidden self-praise.
rows.anchor: فوصف نفسه أولا بما هو فوق علم العلماء وهو الإخبار بالمغيبات

rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: Many authorities take the food's arrival to mean while awake; Ibn Jurayj is also cited for this, while some take it as food arriving in a dream.
rows.anchor: حمل الإتيان على الإتيان في اليقظة ذهب غير واحد من الأجلة

rows.speaker: السدي وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: They say Joseph knew the baker would be killed and spoke of dream food to distract the prisoners and give the doomed man a chance to believe; al-Ālūsī accepts the hope of conversion but rejects the distraction account.
rows.anchor: قال السدي وابن إسحاق : إنه عليه السلام لما علم من رؤية الخباز أنه يقتل

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn Jurayj, transmitted by Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir, says Joseph avoided interpretation out of compassion for the doomed prisoner, then preached monotheism when pressed; al-Ālūsī finds it unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: رواية أخرى عن ابن جريج أخرجها ابن جرير وابن المنذر وغيرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in taʾwīlihi returns to food; taking it as the dreams the prisoners recounted conflicts with the apparent wording and Joseph's purpose, and the other proposed readings are weak.
rows.anchor: فالضمير في تأويله يعود على الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readings take the pronoun as referring to the two dreams or make the food the food they saw in sleep; the former is contrary to the apparent sense and irrelevant to his purpose.
rows.anchor: وجوز على ما قصاه عليه من الرؤيتين على معنى لا يأتيكما طعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph clarifies that his knowledge is divine favor, not soothsaying or astrology; the demonstrative points to the lofty rank of what God taught him.
rows.anchor: ليس من علوم الكهنة والمنجمين بل هو فضل إلهي يؤتيه من يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is reported that the prisoners asked where his knowledge came from; another report says they accused him of soothsaying or astrology.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنهما قالا له : من أين لك ما تدعيه من العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about leaving the unbelievers' religion answers why God taught him; reading it as cause of the relative clause or of the whole report is rejected as unintended.
rows.anchor: استئناف وقع جوابا عن سؤال نشأ مما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving means abstaining, since Joseph never adopted their shirk; the wording gently invites his listeners to abandon their religion too.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالترك الامتناع فإنه لم يتلوث بتلك قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Describing them as people who do not believe in God stresses that worshipping Him alongside idols is not genuine faith in Him.
rows.anchor: للتنصيص على أن عبادتهم له تعالى مع عبادة الأوثان ليس بإيمان به تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people may be those whom the clause describes wherever they were, or Egyptians specifically, who were idolaters then.
rows.anchor: أهل مصر فإنهم كانوا عبدة إذ ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated pronoun in the afterlife clause may restrict that unbelief to the people just described, unlike Canaanites following Abraham's religion; repetition emphasizes their strong denial of resurrection.
rows.anchor: على الخصوص دون غيرهم من الكنعانيين الذين هم على ملة إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob continues the explanation of divine favor and encourages the prisoners toward monotheism; leaving false belief comes before adopting the right one.
rows.anchor: داخل في حيز التعليل كأنه قال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some instead take the first clause as a separate preface to the call and the second as disclosure of Joseph's prophetic lineage; Abū Ḥayyān seems to favor this, but al-Ālūsī rejects it.
rows.anchor: وجوز بعضهم أن لا يكون هناك تعليل وإنما الجملة الأولى مستأنفة

rows.speaker: الأشهب العقيلي والكوفيون
rows.claim: Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī and the Kūfans read ābāʾī with a still yāʾ, a reading also related from Abū ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأشهب العقيلي والكوفيون ( آبائي ) بإسكان الياء وهي مروية عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā kāna lanā means it is unfitting or impossible for prophets, given their strong souls, to associate anything with God; another view means their household, due to divine care.
rows.anchor: ما صح وما استقام فضلا عن الوقوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min may be augmentative with 'anything,' emphasizing totality, or may prohibit any amount of association with God.
rows.anchor: فمن زائدة في المفعول به لتأكيد العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The primary reading makes monotheism a direct divine favor on the prophets and, through them, on people by means of prophethood and revelation.
rows.anchor: من فضل الله علينا أي ناشيء من تأييده لنا بالنبوة والوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the primary reading, saying people are ungrateful means they fail to worship one God; gratitude here is monotheism. The explicit noun replaces a pronoun for clarity and to prevent an exclusionary implication.
rows.anchor: لا يوحدون وحيث عبر عن ذلك بذلك العنوان عبر عن التوحيد الذي يوجبه بالشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the favor God's rational proofs for monotheism, supplied to everyone but ignored by most; Abū al-Suʿūd adds that all received minds and senses for recognizing these signs.
rows.anchor: ذلك التوحيد ناشيء من فضل الله تعالى علينا حيث نصب لنا أدلة ننظر فيها

rows.speaker: المولى أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd says God gave all people minds and senses to use in reflecting on the signs of monotheism in the world and in themselves, yet most do not use them for that purpose.
rows.anchor: حيث أعطانا عقولا ومشاعر نستعملها في دلائل التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility refers dhālika to dream interpretation, a portion of divine favor to Joseph and his forefathers that benefits people through their explanations; al-Ālūsī finds this somewhat remote. Some also suggest prophethood.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون الإشارة إلى ما أشير إليه بذلكما ويراد ما يفهم مما قبل

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām says most people fail to thank God for faith and recounts a debate asking whether faith is God's act; Bishr says gratitude is due for capacity, reason, and means, not faith itself.
rows.anchor: وأوجب الإمام كون المراد في قوله : ( لا يشكرون )

rows.speaker: ثمامة بن الأشرس
rows.claim: Thumāma argues God thanks believers for their deeds rather than believers thanking God for faith, quoting that their striving is appreciated.
rows.anchor: ثمامة بن الأشرس فقال : إنا لا نشكر الله تعالى على الإيمان بل الله تعالى يشكره علينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects Thumāma's view: the verse calls monotheism God's favor and blames most people for not thanking Him, proving believers must thank God for faith.
rows.anchor: بين فيها أن عدم الاشتراك من فضل الله تعالى ثم بين أن أكثر الناس لا يشكرون هذه النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā ṣāḥibayi al-sijn means two companions in prison; the genitive may be an expanded adverbial construction, or companionship may mean residence as with companions of the Fire and Garden.
rows.anchor: أي يا صاحبي فيه إلا أنه أضيف إلى الظرف توسعا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān and other grammarians differ on whether the prison phrase is a quasi-object or object genitive; another view says they are attributed to prison because they are unbelievers, which al-Ālūsī questions.
rows.anchor: والإضافة من باب إضافة الشيء إلى شبه المفعول عند أبي حيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing them as companions in a place of grief may foster affection and counsel and urge truthfulness under hardship; yā, normally marking distance, signals their heedlessness and error.
rows.anchor: والنداء بيا بناءا على الشائع من أنها للبعيد للإشارة إلى غفلتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph gently presents the falsity of inherited beliefs as a question so they will not recoil from abrupt refutation, asking which worship is better.
rows.anchor: وقد تلطف عليه السلام بهما في ردهما إلى الحق وإرشادهما إلى الهدى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān analyzes the syntax as ellipsis: is worshipping scattered lords better for you, or worshipping God the One?
rows.anchor: والكلام على ما صرح به أبو حيان على حذف مضاف أي أعبادة أرباب متفرقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qahhār means the one no one can overpower, which al-Ālūsī prefers to al-Khaṭṭābī's narrower gloss about punishing tyrants and subjecting creation to death.
rows.anchor: الغالب الذي لا يغالبه أحد جل وعلا وهو أولى مما قاله الخطابي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls the contrast a parable of worshipping God alone versus idols; al-Qutb objects that it contrasts many lords with God, then answers by reading God as the one Lord opposite them.
rows.anchor: وذكر الزمخشري إن هذا ضرب لعبادة الله تعالى وحده ولعبادة الأصنام واعترضه القطب

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī objects that the parable is not apparent in the wording; he later proposes supplying the image of several masters owning one slave against a single overpowering master.
rows.anchor: وقال الطيبي أيضا : إن في ذلك إشكالا لأن الظاهر من الآية نفي استواء الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī's proposed comparison is several masters owning one slave versus one overpowering master; al-Kashf says this makes the parable clear.
rows.anchor: لكن التقدير أسادات شتى تستعبد مملوكا واحدا خير من شيد واحد قهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct sense denies parity between idols and God; treating it as a parable requires interpretation but has subtle force and may be preferable.
rows.anchor: والحق أنه ظاهر في نفي الاستواء وإن جعله مثلا يحتاج إلى تأويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scattered may mean many, contrasted with the One, while al-Qahhār answers helplessness; others take it as differing forms, kinds, natures, or lack of agreement, also signifying inability.
rows.anchor: وحمل التفرق في العدد والتكاثر

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām draws several arguments against idols from the verse and apparently does not treat it as a parable; Joseph broadens the address to his companions and people sharing their religion.
rows.anchor: وقد استنبط الإمام من الآية غير ما حجة بطلان عبادة الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objects worshipped besides God are empty names without real referents: people invented the names and worshipped what they claimed they denoted, without proof from reason or revelation.
rows.anchor: ألفاظا فارغة لا مطابق لها في الخارج لأن ما ليس فيه مصداق إطلاق الاسم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even those who claim to worship God while imagining Him as a body on a throne worship their own imagined entity, not God; the true referent of the divine name is beyond that conception.
rows.anchor: لأن ما وضع له الاسم الجليل في نفسه الأمر ليس هو الذي تخيلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God judges worship because He alone deserves it as necessary existent, creator, and owner; the command to worship none but Him follows reason and answers the question raised earlier.
rows.anchor: إلا لله عن سلطانه لأنه المستحق لها بالذات إذ هو الواجب بالذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command may be treated as the reason worship belongs to God alone, but al-Ālūsī calls that causal reading less apparent than the question-and-answer reading.
rows.anchor: وفي موضع التعليل لمحذوف كأنه قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence closes every defense of idols: a claimed divine proof is answered by the lack of authority, a human ruling by God's sole judgment, and supposed neutrality by His command to worship only Him.
rows.anchor: لسد الطرق في توجيه صحة عبادة الأصنام عليهم أحكم سد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-dīn al-qayyim is the established religion demonstrated by rational and transmitted proofs; most people fail to know it and instead follow habit and sense, which leads to anthropomorphism and attributing events to celestial bodies.
rows.anchor: الثابت الذي دلت عليه البراهين العقلية والنقلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People's ignorance may mean failure to recognize those proofs or total ignorance, leading them to worship invented names while turning from reason and revelation.
rows.anchor: لجهلهم تلك البراهين أو لا يعلمون شيئا أصلا فيعبدون أسماء سموها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source of this turning away is attachment to what is familiar and restriction to sensory things, common in human nature.
rows.anchor: ومنشأ هذا الإعراض الوقوف عند المألوف والتقيد بالحسيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ḍighth is a small bundle of mixed plants, less than a sheaf but more than a handful; a poem uses the word for mixed basil, and 38:44 uses it for Job's bundle of palm twigs.
rows.anchor: وهي جمع ضغث وهو أقل من الحزمة وأكثر من القبضة من أخلاط النبات

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf explains confused dreams as mixtures and falsehoods from self-talk or Satan, metaphorically named after bundles of mixed plants.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف أن ( أضغاث الأحلام ) تخاليطها وأباطيلها وما يكون منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says metaphor names both the image and target; one answer treats ḍighth first as an image for mixtures and falsehoods generally, then specifies them as dreams.
rows.anchor: الأول أنه يريد أن حقيقة الأضغاث أخلاط النبات فشبه به التخاليط والأباطيل مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In that analysis, the dream and the king's vision are outside the two sides of the metaphor, so their mention does not invalidate it.
rows.anchor: فالأحلام ورؤيا الملك خارجان عنهما فلا يضر ذكرهما

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: A second defense says ḍighths are confused components within one dream, not the dream itself, like calling a cheek a rose; al-Ālūsī finds this strained and non-apparent.
rows.anchor: الثاني أن الأضغاث استعيرت للتخاليط الواقعة في الرؤيا الواحدة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the expression as the figure 'silver of water,' avoiding the objection to al-Zamakhsharī, though al-Ālūsī says the lexical precedent does not clearly support it.
rows.anchor: واستظهر بعضهم كون ( أضغاث أحلام ) من قبيل لجين الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say ruʾyā and ḥulm both mean anything seen in sleep, though usage favors ruʾyā for good and ḥulm for bad; a prophetic report distinguishes vision from God and dream from Satan.
rows.anchor: الرؤيا والحلم عبارة عما يراه النائم مطلقا لكن غلبت الرؤيا

rows.speaker: التوربشتي
rows.claim: Al-Turbushtī says Arabs used the terms alike, while the Prophet distinguished true visions from false satanic dreams; the word ḥulm suggests an unreal imagined fulfillment of desire.
rows.anchor: وقال التوربشتي : الحلم عند العرب يستعمل استعمال الرؤيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural aḥlām is emphatic although the king had one dream, as when one person is said to ride horses despite owning a single horse.
rows.anchor: بالجمع مع أن الرؤيا ما كانت إلا واحدة للمبالغة في وصف ذلك بالبطلان

rows.speaker: الفرائد
rows.claim: Al-Farāʾid says one dream contains many components, each a dream; al-Shihāb calls this explanation weak although al-Ṭībī liked it.
rows.anchor: وفي الفرائد لما كانت ( أضغاث أحلام ) مستعارة لما ذكر

rows.speaker: الرضي
rows.claim: Al-Raḍī says a broken plural normally indicates small number rather than mere plurality; the author notes that a plural with no competing plural can function as a general plural.
rows.anchor: ثم نقل عن الرضي أنه قال في شرح الشافية إن جمع القلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression aḍghāth fits especially well beside the grain ears in the dream, showing the Qur'an's rhetorical artistry.
rows.anchor: حسن موقع الأضغاث مع السنابل فيا لله در شأن التنزيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may mean the dream is false and has no interpretation, or use al for false dreams specifically; this gives a premise excusing their ignorance, like a cited Arabic construction.
rows.anchor: لأنها لا تأويل لها وإنما التأويل للمنامات الصادقة

rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munīr prefers taking dreams generically: the court admits it lacks interpretive skill, matching the king's uncertainty and the messenger's hope that people will learn.
rows.anchor: واختاره ابن المنير وادعى أنه الظاهر وأن قول الملك لهم أولا

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some say the advisers' shift from the king's term taʿbīr to taʾwīl implies interpretive effort beyond moving from sign to meaning; the phrase about confused dreams might reassure the king.
rows.anchor: يشعر به عدو لهم عما وقع في كلام الملك من العبارة المعبرة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf reads two independent points: the dream is confused, and the advisers are skilled in counsel rather than dream interpretation; this fits a court because few master that art.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الكشف : إن وجه ذلك أن يجعل الأول جوابا مستقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits sending the messenger; he reaches Joseph and calls him ṣiddīq, having observed his truth in prison. This opening teaches an asker to honor the person consulted.
rows.anchor: فأتاه فقال : يا يوسف ووصفه بالمبالغة في الصدق حسبما علمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording suggests the prisoners' dreams were genuine; it is the statement that they had lied that may have been false, if established.
rows.anchor: واستدل بذلك على أنهما لم يكذبا على يوسف في منامهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger asks for a fatwā about the dream's outcome without naming it because context makes it clear; aftinā rather than nabbiʾnā honors Joseph's rank.
rows.anchor: وإنما لم يصرح به لوضوح مرامه بقرينة ما سبق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural request suggests the dream concerns others and public affairs, with the messenger serving as interpreter and envoy.
rows.anchor: إشعارا بأن الرؤيا ليست له بل لغيره ممن له ملابسة بأمور العامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger may return to the king and court or to the people of the town, reporting Joseph's interpretation so they learn its meaning or his merit and help free him.
rows.anchor: أي إلى الملك ومن عنده أو إلى أهل البلد فأنبئهم بما أفتيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says laʿalla politely rather than promising a return or understanding he cannot guarantee; people may fail to understand or trust him.
rows.anchor: وإنما لم يبت القول بل قال : ( لعلي ) و ( لعلهم ) مجاراة معه عليه السلام

rows.speaker: غير واحد
rows.claim: Many take dhālika to refer to verification and the preceding events as a whole; Joseph's request was to clear his name, and the concise narration omits the messenger's return and the king's inquiry.
rows.anchor: ذهب إليه غير واحد أن ذلك إشارة إلى التثبت مع ما تلاه من القصة أجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the preferred reading, Joseph is speaking and al-ʿAzīz should know that Joseph did not betray his household trust while the master was absent.
rows.anchor: فعند ذلك قال عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatives make 'know' refer to the king and 'betray' to al-ʿAzīz, or make both refer to the king because a minister's betrayal counts as the king's betrayal.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ضمير ( يعلم ) للملك وضمير ( أخنه ) للعزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in bi-l-ghayb may indicate circumstance or location: Joseph did not betray him while he was away, or behind curtains and locked doors.
rows.anchor: والباء إما للملابسة أو للظرفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not guide a traitor's scheme means He does not carry it through or strengthen it; guidance is metaphorical for execution, or the cause is named for its authors.
rows.anchor: أي لا ينفذه ولا يسدده بل يبطله ويزهقه فهداية الكيد مجاز عن تنفيذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saying alludes to the wife's betrayal of al-ʿAzīz's trust and the minister's betrayal of God by imprisoning Joseph despite signs of innocence, and also affirms Joseph's fidelity.
rows.anchor: وفيه تعريض بارأة العزيز في خيانتها أمانته وبه في خيانته أمانة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph calls his persistent effort a scheme only hypothetically, if it were betrayal; al-Kashf's suggestion of metaphor or wordplay is unsound.
rows.anchor: وتسميته كيدا على فرض الخيانة على بابها حقيقة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view makes both pronouns refer to God: the point is to manifest Joseph's innocence and raise his standing; the phrase is compared with God's disclosure of who follows the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن ضمير ( يعلم ) و ( لم أخنه ) لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's words express humility, avoid self-congratulation, or acknowledge that virtue comes from God's favor rather than the soul acting by its own nature; the phrasing resembles the Prophet's claim to be leader of Adam's children, without boasting.
rows.anchor: هضما لنفسه البرية عن كل سوء وتواضعا لله تعالى وتحاشيا عن التزكية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says Joseph meant that his abstention came from fear of God, not from lack of natural desire.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه أشار بذلك إلى أن عدم التعرض لم يكن لعدم الميل الطبيعي

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report from Anas, raised to the Prophet and also related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ḥakīm ibn Jābir, al-Ḥasan, and others, says Gabriel asked whether Joseph felt desire; if sound, desire means inclination rather than resolve.
rows.anchor: وقد أخرجه الحاكم في تاريخه وابن مردويه بلفظ قريب من هذا عن أنس مرفوعا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some allow the report to mean actual resolve, treating it as a minor sin prophets could commit before prophethood, so Joseph was not yet a prophet; al-Zamakhsharī condemns such stories as fabrications.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لا مانع من أن يحمل على الثاني ويقال : إنه صغيرة وهي تجوز على الأنبياء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says most commentators treat the exception as disconnected and mā as a verbal noun: only the Lord's mercy turns evil away from the soul.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية : الجمهور على أن الاستثناء منقطع و ( ما ) مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammatical account makes the exception temporal: the soul urges evil except in times of divine mercy and protection; objections follow if this means prophets are inclined to desire through most of life.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون استثناء من أعم الأوقات و ( ما ) مصدرية ظرفية زمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other analyses except a soul God protects, the subject of 'urges,' or the person urged; the last makes mā refer to a rational being, which is unusual. Al-Ālūsī favors the initial account and explains God's names as forgiveness of natural impulses and protection from acting on them.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون استثناء من النفس أو من الضمير المستتر في أمارة الراجع إليها

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī, with Abū Ḥayyān favoring this as apparent, makes the words from 'that, so he may know' through 'I do not exonerate myself' part of the wife's confession: she did not betray Joseph, yet admits her wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وذهب الجبائي واستظهره أبو حيان إلى أن ( ذلك ليعلم ) إلى هنا من كلام امرأة العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kashf objects that this view rests only on imagined surface continuity: after the case is clear, the wife would hardly say 'I do not exonerate myself.'
rows.anchor: ليس موجبه إلا ماتوهم من الاتصال الصوري

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: Supporters say this reading makes the purpose clause more direct: the wife wants Joseph to know she did not betray him while absent, yet her soul urged evil; she seeks forgiveness and mercy.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من انتصر له بأن أمر التعليل ظاهر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī answers that Joseph aimed at complete public vindication: the king already suspected the truth but had not acted, and inquiry before release made his innocence fully known while respecting al-ʿAzīz's rights.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن المراد ليظهر علمه على أتم وجه وهو يستدعي الخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The procedure could make the king act on knowledge he already had, stop maligning Joseph, and honor him publicly; such tactics can serve prophetic outreach, like favoring a leader to promote the mission.
rows.anchor: إن في التثبت وتقديم التفتيش على الخروج من مراعاة حقوق العزيز ما فيه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One suggestion says Joseph acted to prevent al-ʿAzīz from maligning him to the king, but al-Ālūsī considers a choice inviting even mild blame remote; he prefers that Joseph used the moment to call people to God and make amends for a lapse in judgment.
rows.anchor: وقيل هنا : إن ذلك لئلا يقبح العزيز أمره عند الملك

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the Qur'an uses prolepsis, joining the words to Joseph's earlier request that the king ask about the women; al-Ālūsī says this apparent reading raises an obvious problem.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج أن هذا من تقديم القرآن وتأخيره

rows.speaker: البزي وقالون
rows.claim: Al-Bazzī from Ibn Kathīr and Qālūn from Nāfiʿ read al-sūʾ with the hamza changed into wāw and assimilated.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية البزي عن ابن كثير وقالون عن نافع أنهما قرآ
